title: Slirc docs
text: Slirc documentation Slack, without giving up IRC. Slirc combines familiar team chat with an open protocol and hardware you control. Your coding agent can join too: Pi, Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode work today, and more are coming. These guides explain the app and what stays available from ordinary IRC clients. Getting startedJoin with your email, say hi in #open-chat, and sign in on your other devices. DownloadThe Mac and iPhone apps, and installing Slirc from the browser on Windows, Android and Linux. AgentsConnect a Pi, Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode session and talk to it from your phone. Channels & invitesHow channels and direct messages work, and how invite links get you in. Messages & mediaSend, format, react, edit, and share images, videos, and links. ThreadsTurn one message into a focused conversation that stays portable. NotificationsChoose when Slirc should get your attention across your devices. IRC clientsHalloy, Senpai, WeeChat, Textual, and Revolution IRC, with a password or a certificate. BotsThe @remind, @help and @poll helpers, and IRC accounts for your own scripts. Privacy & safetyWhere your data lives, how access is gated, and what stays private. Self-hostingRun Slirc on your own server, from a fresh Linux box to your first message. FootprintMeasured RAM, CPU, and disk next to Campfire, and the server ladder that follows. FAQCost, IRC clients, agents, deletion, iPhone push, and group size.

title: Slirc docs
heading: What is Slirc?
text: Slirc is a self-hosted team chat. The app, in the browser or on Mac and iPhone, gives you channels, direct messages, reactions, threads, media, and notifications. Ergo IRC handles accounts, rooms, permissions, messages, reactions, and history. Scripts, bots and your coding agent join as ordinary members. Everything stays legible in an ordinary IRC client. Threads are channels, uploads are URLs, and history does not depend on one proprietary interface.

title: Slirc docs
heading: How to use these guides
text: Start with Getting started to sign in, and Download to get the app on your devices. The rest of the guides map to what you do day to day: Channels & invites: channels, direct messages, and invitation links. Messages & media: formatting, reactions, edits, uploads, and previews. Threads: focused replies that stay in their channel as standard IRC +reply messages. Notifications: choosing when Slirc gets your attention. Agents: connect your coding agent. Pi, Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode work today. Bots: the @remind, @help and @poll helpers, and IRC accounts your own scripts log in as. IRC clients: connecting a terminal or desktop client. Privacy & safety: data, access boundaries, and account safety. Self-hosting: running Slirc on your own server. FAQ: short answers to the questions people bring first.

title: Slirc docs
heading: Note
text: Looking for a specific command? The /help command inside the app lists everything available.

title: Getting started
text: Sign up on a public instance or join from an invite email, and start chatting in a couple of minutes. Every step works on desktop and phone.

title: Getting started
heading: Join a public instance
text: On a public instance, open #open-chat and read along. When you want to post, tap the message box or choose Sign in to post. Type your email and, if you're new, what we should call you. Then open the link in the email, or type its code; pasting the code with its space works. You land in #open-chat. Your nick comes from the name you typed, without spaces or symbols. Staff names like admin aren't available. A new account belongs to #open-chat and #help only, plus its DM with help, until someone invites it somewhere else. A signup nobody confirms within two hours is dropped.

title: Getting started
heading: Join from your invite
text: Open the link in your invite email. Pick a display name and choose Join Slirc. If a friend invited you, the button says Join. There's no password to set. If you were invited to a channel, you land in it. Help sends you a DM with a link to your first steps. Reply there with any question about Slirc, any time. Your display name also becomes your nick, the @handle next to your messages. You can change your display name any time under You; your nick stays the same. Staff and helper names, and the names of admins, agents and bots, aren't available.

title: Getting started
heading: Say hi in #open-chat
text: Open #open-chat under Channels, in the sidebar on desktop or on Home on a phone. Type your message at the bottom and press Enter or the send button. On a phone, pull down at the top of Home, More or a conversation to check you're up to date. Slirc confirms the connection, reconnects if it dropped, and fetches anything new. With no network it says you're offline.

title: Getting started
heading: Make a channel
text: Choose + next to Channels, in the desktop sidebar or on phone Home. Give it a name and pick Invite-only or Open. Only people you invite can see an invite-only channel. Open channels are listed for every member to join. Choose Create channel. You land in the new channel, ready to invite people.

title: Getting started
heading: Bring a friend
text: In a channel, type /invite friend@example.com and choose Invite by email in the note that appears. Your friend gets an email with a link to join that channel. To start a DM, choose + next to Direct messages, in the desktop sidebar or on the phone DMs screen. Type a name to find someone who's already here, or an email address to invite someone new and choose Send invite. The dialog shows how many email invites you have left; admins have no limit.

title: Getting started
heading: Send messages, photos, GIFs and videos
text: Messages: press Enter to send and Shift + Enter for a new line. Markdown basics like **bold** and *italic* work too. Photos: choose + beside the message box and pick up to 10 JPEG, PNG or WebP photos, each under 12 MB. You can also paste photos into the message box, and on desktop drop them onto the conversation or the message box. GIFs: type /giphy and a word, like /giphy hello, then pick a GIF. Videos: choose + beside the message box and pick an MP4, MOV or WebM video. A large video is compressed to about 720p before upload and has to end up under 30 MB. It plays right in the conversation. Longer videos are better shared as a YouTube, Vimeo or Loom link, which also plays inline.

title: Getting started
heading: Start threads and react
text: To keep a side conversation out of the channel, type /threads followed by your reply. That starts a thread from the latest message. On desktop you can also hover any message, choose ⋮, then Reply in thread. Your threads appear under Threads in the sidebar or on Home. To react on desktop, hover a message and choose the smile button. On any device, tap a reaction under a message to add yours, and tap it again to take it back.

title: Getting started
heading: Change your profile picture
text: Choose your avatar, at the bottom of the sidebar on desktop or at the top right on a phone. Choose the picture at the top of your profile and pick an image. Your new profile picture saves right away.

title: Getting started
heading: Turn on notifications
text: Open your profile by choosing your avatar on desktop, or More → Profile on a phone. Choose Change beside Notifications and allow them when your browser asks. On iPhone, add Slirc to your Home Screen first (see below); notifications only arrive in the Home Screen app.

title: Getting started
heading: Good to know
text: Only members post in #open-chat and #help. On a public instance, a visitor who isn't signed in can read recent #open-chat messages at /open-chat: the text, who wrote it and when, and nothing else. Only signed-in members can read #help, and it keeps participant presence hidden in the Slirc app. Questions, bugs or ideas? Ask @help or message your instance's admin inside Slirc. For more detail, read channels and invites and messages and media.

title: Getting started
heading: Save Slirc to your Home Screen
text: Once it's on your Home Screen, Slirc opens from its icon, like any other app.

title: Getting started
heading: iPhone
text: Open Slirc in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. If your instance offers the iPhone app in TestFlight, signed-in members find the link under More → Get the iPhone app on a phone; it has no notifications yet. See Download for details.

title: Getting started
heading: Android
text: Open the browser menu and choose Add to Home screen or Install app.

title: Getting started
heading: Add your phone
text: On a computer where you're signed in, choose Add your phone in the sidebar, or open Devices from your profile and choose Show code. A QR code appears. Point your phone's camera at it and open the link. The phone signs in to the same account, with nothing to type. The code works once and lasts a minute. A fresh one replaces it while the card stays open. When the phone gets in, the card names its browser and system. If that wasn't you, choose Not you? Sign it out. If you saved Slirc to your iPhone Home Screen, open that app and choose Scan to sign in on its sign-in screen. The Home Screen app keeps its own sign-in, separate from Safari, so it has its own scanner.

title: Getting started
heading: Sign in on another device
text: On the new device, open Slirc and choose Link with another device, or Use a code instead on a phone. Type the code it shows under Devices on a device where you're already signed in, then choose Review and Approve. No other device handy? Enter your email, choose Send sign-in link, and open the link from that email on the new device.

title: Download and install
text: Install the Slirc app on your Mac, iPhone, or any browser, or connect an IRC client. The same channels everywhere.

title: Download and install
heading: Mac
text: The Mac app is built from the desktop/ directory in the repository for macOS 14 or later. If your operator distributes a signed DMG, open it and drag Slirc to Applications. On first launch, enter any verified HTTPS Slirc instance address (hosted or self-hosted). Up to six workspaces stay live in one window, and Switch Workspace… in the Slirc menu (Option-Cmd-O) or the left workspace rail switches between them. The Mac app has no notifications yet. If you want them, install Slirc from the browser as below.

title: Download and install
heading: iPhone
text: The iPhone app is built from the native/ directory and can be distributed through TestFlight, Apple's app for test builds. When your instance configures TESTFLIGHT_URL, signed-in members find the install link under More → Get the iPhone app on a phone. Install TestFlight from the App Store. Open the TestFlight link your instance provides. Tap Install. Open Slirc and enter any verified HTTPS Slirc instance address (hosted or self-hosted). The iPhone app has no notifications yet. For notifications, add Slirc to the Home Screen from Safari instead. Open your instance, tap the share button, then Add to Home Screen. Getting started has a video.

title: Download and install
heading: Windows, Android and Linux
text: Open your instance in the browser, sign in, and install it as an app. Each instance gets its own window and icon. In Edge, open the ⋯ menu, then More tools, Apps and Install this site as an app. In Chrome, open the ⋮ menu, then Cast, save and share and Install page as app. In Chrome on Android, open the ⋮ menu, tap Add to home screen, then Install. An Android app is planned. Firefox on Linux can't install web apps, so there Slirc stays a browser tab.

title: Download and install
heading: IRC clients
text: IRC clients like Halloy connect to any Slirc instance over TLS. Set one up.

title: Download and install
heading: Start at login
text: To open Slirc when you sign in to your computer, find it in chrome://apps or edge://apps and turn on start at login.

title: Download and install
heading: Notifications on Windows and Linux
text: Open the installed Slirc window and turn notifications on in your profile there, as on the notifications page. In a browser tab, Edge only allows them while the tab is open. In the installed app they arrive while the browser runs, even with the Slirc window closed. Edge keeps running in the background on Windows. In Chrome, turn on Continue running background apps when Google Chrome is closed under Settings, System.

title: Channels & invites
text: Channels hold group conversations. Open channels are listed for every registered user; invite-only channels only appear once you're invited.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Channels
text: Slirc uses IRC channels for group chat. Three kinds: The public help channel, open to every registered member. Open channels, listed for every registered user. Invite-only channels, invisible until you're invited. Verified members can create both kinds. The rooms panel shows rooms you belong to, open channels you can join, threads, direct messages, and a Starred section for channels and DMs you pin on this device.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Public help channel
text: The public help channel is open to every registered member. Members can read it; writing requires an account. Slirc does not currently offer anonymous reading. In the Slirc app, its member list, joins, parts, and quits stay hidden. Slirc does not yet promise IRC invisibility, so ordinary IRC clients connected to the channel may still see who is present.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Open channels
text: Verified members can create an open channel for the whole group. Every registered user can see it and join. Use it for a topic the group shares, like a project room or an event.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Invite-only channels
text: Verified members can create an invite-only channel, and an owner or admin can switch a channel between open and invite-only later. Making a channel open again exposes its whole history to every registered member; the hint under the choice says so before you save. An invite-only channel is invisible to everyone who hasn't been invited. The app only lists channels you belong to, and the server blocks anyone who isn't on the list.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Direct messages
text: Choose + beside Direct messages to start a conversation. Search verified people by nick or name. help and remind show up in Contacts and in search too, when your server runs them. Admins are visible contacts for every verified member, even without a shared room. Admins can search and message any verified person in the system. Other people appear through membership in a public or workspace channel, a post in a public channel (including #open-chat and #help), a shared non-direct room, or a DM you have had with them, even a closed one. Contacts, listed before you type, include anyone you have a DM with and leave out people you only share #open-chat or #help with; search still finds them. Select one person to open your existing DM or create one. Discovering a person does not grant access to their private channels or other DMs. Existing groups use secret IRC channels, not pair DMs, and cannot be made open. Group creation is not currently offered in the New DM picker. New members can read the group's existing history; adding people never exposes an earlier 1:1 conversation. You can also open a person's profile by clicking their name, or use /msg: /msg nick Hello there Direct messages appear under Direct messages in the rooms panel. Use a row's menu to star or unstar, mute or unmute, or close a DM; starred conversations also appear at the top of the rooms panel. Mute dims the conversation mark on this device and does not change push-notification settings. Close DM hides the one-to-one conversation from your list on all your devices. It does not delete messages or change the shared IRC channel, membership, or the other person's view. A new message in a closed DM reopens it. You can also open it again from Contacts, with history intact. Slirc backs each direct message with a hidden private #dm-* IRC channel shared by both people, so messages arrive even if the other person is offline. The PWA shows the person's name and avatar; terminal clients see the private channel and its readable topic.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Notes
text: Notes sits at the top of Direct messages, on phone and desktop. It is a private scratchpad, like a DM with yourself. Write in the usual box, and links get previews. Use a note's menu to edit or delete it. Opening /dm/<your nick> opens Notes too. Notes are not messages. They stay in the Slirc app's database, never go over IRC, and nobody else can see them, admins included. IRC clients do not show them. They have no unread counts or notifications, and they show on all your signed-in devices. To add an image to a note, paste, pick or drop it. It shows above the box and uploads when you save the note. Only you can open it.

title: Channels & invites
heading: The channel menu
text: Every non-thread channel in the rooms panel has a kebab menu (⋮). Opening another menu or picker closes the previous one. It holds the actions you take on the spot: Star: pins the channel to the Starred section at the top of your rooms on this device. The same action is available for direct messages. DM menus also offer View profile, Mute and Close DM; View profile opens that person's card. Mute: keeps the channel visible but dims its mark on this device. It does not change push notifications; see notifications. Copy: opens a submenu with Name and Link. Name and Link copy the channel name or a link to the channel. The link opens the channel in Slirc for people who already have access. Leave channel: non-owners. Drops you out of the channel. Owners keep the channel; transferring ownership isn't available yet, so an owner either keeps it or deletes it. Members: the desktop panel starts closed. Open it from the people icon in the header. Everyone in the channel, grouped online, away, and offline, with the owner, admins, agents, and bots marked; select a member to open their profile. Collapse it with the header icon or the panel's hide button. Open channels do not list members, and #help keeps participant presence private. Invite-only channels also show your Pending invitations, without counting invitees as members. Other members cannot see the email addresses you invited. Channel settings…: opens the channel settings dialog.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Channel settings
text: The dialog's title names the channel. Any member can change the Topic. Owners and admins also pick the Visibility: Open lists the channel for every registered member and makes its history readable; Invite-only hides the channel and requires an invite from then on. The hint under the choice describes only the one you picked. Save stays off until something changes, then saves the topic and visibility together. The channel's owner and admins also see Archive channel. After you confirm, the channel turns read-only. Members still read its history and it stays in their list, but the composer is replaced by an Archived channel bar and nobody can post, from Slirc or from an IRC client. The heading says Archived · read only. Choose Unarchive in the same place to let people post again. DMs and threads can't be archived, and neither can the default channel or an open playground channel. Admins also see Delete channel below. You type the channel name to confirm. Deleting removes the channel for everyone, with its messages, threads, memberships, invites and files; anyone who had it open moves to the default channel with a short notice. The default channel and DMs can't be deleted.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Browsing and joining open channels
text: Open channels you haven't joined show up under Browse channels in the rooms panel. Pick one and join, no invite needed. Archived channels don't appear there.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Creating a channel
text: Verified members create either kind from the same form, with + beside Channels in the desktop sidebar or on phone Home. It defaults to invite-only.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Inviting people
text: In a channel, type /invite @eve to add someone who is already on Slirc. A note at the bottom of the channel says Add @eve to #design? with Add and Dismiss; Add adds them right away, and the note changes to Added @eve. If they're already a member, the note says so. Only you see these notes, and they go away when you reload. Channel permissions still apply: if you can't add people to the channel, the note says @eve isn't in #design. You can't add people here. and has no Add. Mentioning someone works the same way. If you @mention a person who isn't in an invite-only channel, a note under your message says @eve isn't in #design. with Add and Dismiss. Mentions in DMs, of bots, and of people who are already in the channel don't show a note. To add your agent, type /invite @claude-8fe7 (its nick) in an open or invite-only channel, then mention it there. Only you can invite your own agents. An open-channel attachment is owner-only: it acts only on your messages, so someone else mentioning it does nothing, it reads the channel's history, and it leaves when you do. See Agents. /invite name@example.com shows a note that says Send name@example.com an invitation to #design?. Nothing is sent until you choose Invite by email; the note then says Invitation sent to name@example.com. If the address already belongs to someone on Slirc, they're added to the channel instead. When you have no email invites left, or haven't verified your own email yet, the note says so and has no button. For a DM, open + beside Direct messages and enter a name or email in the same field. Choosing a person opens the DM immediately; an email requires Send invite. Email invitations are personal, not reusable channel links. Group creation is not offered in this picker. If an address matches an existing verified member, Slirc opens the DM or adds them to the selected group/channel, subject to your permissions. It sends no email and spends no invitation credit, even when your allowance is empty. Selecting a person and entering their email does not add them twice. The default allowance is nine invitation emails per verified account, shared across DMs, groups and channels. Your server may set a different limit; the dialog shows it. Admins have no allowance, so the dialog and People show Unlimited email invites for them. Inviting the same email again to the same destination reuses its active invitation without sending another email or spending another credit. Explicit resends count, and cancelling a delivered invitation does not refund its credit. Confirmed delivery failures do not consume credit. An uncertain delivery keeps its credit and cannot be resent blindly. Open People from your profile navigation or More → Invitations on a phone to see your sent invitations, remaining allowance, and delivery status. You can resend eligible invitations or cancel a pending invitation. Cancellation revokes the link, not existing conversation membership. A desktop Invite someone shortcut opens the new-conversation dialog for people or email recipients; its dismiss (×) hides only that shortcut. Email invitations expire after seven days and require the invited email account. Resending replaces the link and starts a new seven-day window. Invitations are personal to the invited address, so forward the email only to the person it names. An invited person is an ordinary IRC participant. IRC clients see the same private channels, access grants and conversation history.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Invitations are personal
text: Only the invited email address can accept an invitation, and it expires after seven days. Send invitations to people you trust, and cancel one if you sent it to the wrong address.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Inviting many people
text: Admins can invite a whole list in one go. Open People and choose Invite many, or choose Invite many in the new-conversation dialog. Under Invite to, pick a channel you belong to, or Workspace only, which uses the default channel everyone joins. With no channel to pick, the dialog skips this choice. Then paste addresses, one per line, or drop a CSV file. Any column that holds email addresses works, names are optional, and a header row is skipped. Check list shows what happens to each address before anything is sent. A new address gets an email invite. Someone already on Slirc is added to the channel, or marked as already there. An address you invited to the same place is marked Already invited and gets no second email. Repeats, typos and your own address are marked and left out. Someone on Slirc you can't find in People is added too, but the list shows only their address. Send sends the invites in batches and shows progress, so keep the dialog open until it finishes. The summary lists each address with its result, and the Copy button copies the addresses that were not sent. Bulk invites use up to 75% of the server's daily email limit, which leaves room for sign-in emails. When a list is bigger than what's left today, the extra addresses wait; check the list again the next day to send them. Each invitation then works like any other: it expires after seven days, and People shows it under Sent invitations.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Join links
text: An admin can make one link that anyone can use to join a channel, for example to post in a group chat. Open People and use Join link: pick the channel, choose Make link and copy it. To send it again later, use Copy link next to the open link. Links made before 19 Nov 2026 can't be copied again; make a new one instead. Opening the link asks for an email address and sends one email. Someone new picks a name and lands in the channel; an address that already has an account signs in instead. If you are signed in and already in the channel, the link opens the channel. A link takes 99 people and lasts seven days. People shows how many joined, and Revoke closes the link at once.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Kicking someone from a channel
text: An admin can type /kick @eve in a channel to take that person out of it. A reason can follow the nick, as in /kick @eve posting spam. They leave the channel right away, and the channel shows a line from you, like removed eve from #design: posting spam. IRC clients also see the kick. To come back to an invite-only channel they need a new invite; an open channel they can join again from Browse channels. Admins can't kick themselves or another admin, and /kick doesn't work in a channel everyone belongs to, like #open-chat. Only admins see /kick in the command list.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Removing a member
text: An admin can remove a person from the workspace: open their profile, choose Remove member, and confirm. They leave every channel, thread and DM, every device they signed in on is signed out, and IRC clients lose their password and certificates. They can't sign in again or come back through a join link or invitation with the same email. Their past messages stay under their name. Any admin can do this. Admins can't remove themselves or another admin, and agents and bots are managed from their own pages.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Workspace icon
text: An admin can give the workspace its own icon. Open Admin, choose Upload icon under Branding and pick a PNG, JPEG or WebP image. Drag it inside the square and zoom with the slider, then choose Save icon. The icon takes the place of the letter tile in the sidebar and in the Workspaces list, also in other workspaces that list this one. Other people see it within a minute. Remove brings the letter tile back.

title: Channels & invites
heading: Joining through an invite
text: For an email invitation: Open the link and choose a display name. Choose Join. Slirc signs you in and opens the inviter's DM or the invited group/channel. The link was sent to the invited address, so opening it counts as verifying that email; you cannot substitute another one. If the invited address already has a Slirc account, Slirc emails it a sign-in code and link instead, so a forwarded invitation cannot open that account. Type the code on the invitation page, or open the link. If you are already signed in with the invited account, choose Join directly. If a different account is signed in, switch accounts first.

title: Channels & invites
heading: How it maps to IRC
text: Slirc channels are ordinary IRC channels, so the mechanics are standard IRC under the surface: Concept IRC Open channel registered-only (+R), so guests and unregistered nicks can't join Invite-only channel secret and invite-only (+si), hidden from lists and blocked without an invite Archive moderated (+m), so nobody can post. Members still read it, and it stays in the list Delete unregisters the channel; its name becomes reusable after the channel empties

title: Channels & invites
heading: Switching and ordering channels
text: Open or close the rooms panel with the panel button beside the Slirc mark in the top-left. The heading in the middle shows the current channel or person. On desktop it opens channel settings, or the person's card for a direct message. On a phone it returns to Home. Unread messages show a count on each room. On desktop, drag any channel in Channels up or down to set your own order, or focus a channel and press Alt + ↑ / ↓ (Option + ↑ / ↓ on a Mac). The order saves per account in this browser.

title: Channels & invites
heading: GitHub project channels
text: Verified members can bind a GitHub repository (owner/repo) to a channel through POST /api/projects, which creates or adopts #repo (or #owner-repo) and returns a webhook URL and secret. Signed GitHub webhooks (X-Hub-Signature-256) then post issue and pull request updates straight into the channel. Read next: messages and media, or threads for focused conversations.

title: Messages & media
text: Send text, reactions, images, videos, and links. Everything stays compact and readable, in the app and in any IRC client.

title: Messages & media
heading: Sending a message
text: Type in the composer at the bottom and press Enter to send. Press Shift + Enter for a new line. Inside an open code fence, Enter adds a line and Cmd/Ctrl + Enter sends. Sending closes an unfinished fence for you. The composer always shows which room you're writing to. Saving, queued, and sending labels use muted text with three moving dots. Queued means the message is waiting to send, not that it failed. Reduced motion keeps the dots still. On desktop, press ↑ in an empty composer to select the newest message, and ↑ or ↓ to move between messages. On a selected message, E edits it, D asks to delete it, Q quotes it, T opens its thread and R opens the reaction picker. Esc, or ↓ past the newest message, goes back to the composer. Type / in the composer to pick a command. Press Alt + ↑ (Option + ↑ on a Mac) in the composer to bring back a message you sent earlier in this conversation, like a shell's history. Press it again to go further back, and Alt + ↓ to come forward; past the newest one you get back what you were typing. The recalled text is a new message: change it and send it. To fix a message already sent, use plain ↑ and E instead, which edits it in place. Press Cmd + K (Ctrl + K on Windows and Linux) anywhere to jump to a channel, DM or person. Type part of a name, even a few letters in order such as dvt for dev-test, move with ↑ and ↓, press Enter to open it, or Esc to go back where you were. Conversations with unread messages come first. Press Cmd + Option + O (Ctrl + Alt + O on Windows and Linux) to open the Workspaces list, the same list the workspace icon opens, and switch to another workspace. On a wide screen the rail on the far left lists every saved workspace as an icon; select one to switch, or + at its foot to add one.

title: Messages & media
heading: Starting a direct message
text: Open New DM, type at least two characters to search by name or nick, and choose a person to open the conversation immediately. Choosing a Contact does the same. Type or paste an email in the same field to show an invitation confirmation, then choose Send invite. Typing an email never sends an invitation. After a successful send, the dialog shows confirmation instead of the form; choose Done or Invite someone else. Slirc creates the private pair in the background while you type. The opened conversation is keyed to that person's account, so your draft is saved and anything you send waits locally, then goes out once the server authorizes the conversation. If starting it fails, your text stays in the conversation and Try again retries the same pair instead of creating a second one. Photos wait until the conversation is ready.

title: Messages & media
heading: Typing
text: While someone else types, their avatar appears above the composer with three dots. Only people in the current conversation show. Typing is live only. It is never saved with message history, and replaying older messages never shows it. Your own typing travels on the same IRC connection and clears when you send, pause, or leave the conversation.

title: Messages & media
heading: Formatting
text: Slirc supports a small, safe Markdown subset. Formatting previews in the composer and stays readable as plain text in IRC clients. Style Type Result Bold **important** or __important__ important Italic *gentle* or _gentle_ gentle Inline code `npm install` npm install Code block Fenced with ```; add language after opening fence Glow-highlighted block Link [label](https://…) a label Quote > at the start of a line Quote block List - , * , • or 1. at the start of a line Bulleted or numbered item In a list, a new line starts with the next bullet or number. That's Shift + Enter on a computer and Return on a phone. A new line on an empty item ends the list. Select text and press Cmd/Ctrl + B for bold, Cmd/Ctrl + I for italic, or Cmd/Ctrl + Alt + C for inline code. With no selection, shortcut wraps the word at the caret. Paste an HTTP(S) URL over selected text to make a link. Click or tap a rendered link to open it in a new tab. Right-click it, or long-press it on a phone, for Go to or Edit; Edit selects its text in the composer so pasting a replacement URL keeps its label.

title: Messages & media
heading: Emoji
text: Type :clap: or :claps: for 👏. After two characters, such as :cl, the composer suggests emoji. Use the arrow keys and Enter or Tab to choose; Escape closes the picker without sending. Standard emoji are sent as Unicode, so IRC clients can display them too. Existing custom emoji appear as images in Slirc and keep their :shortcode: on IRC. Code and URLs stay unchanged; unknown shortcodes stay as text.

title: Messages & media
heading: Reactions
text: Hover or focus a message and click the smile button to open the reaction picker. On a phone, touch and hold the message instead; quick reactions sit at the top of the sheet that opens. For any other emoji, choose Add reaction (the smile with a plus) after the quick reactions, type a name such as tada, and press Enter or tap a result. Pick an emoji to stamp the message; tap the stamp again to remove it. Hover or keyboard-focus a stamp to see who added it. Everyone in Slirc sees reactions, and IRC clients with reaction support, such as Halloy, render the same stamps. Custom emoji added to your Slirc show up in message and reaction search. They travel over IRC as readable shortcodes such as :party_parrot:.

title: Messages & media
heading: Editing and deleting
text: Open a message's menu (⋮) or right-click any message on desktop to edit it, reply in a thread, set a reminder with Remind me, copy a link to it with Copy link, or delete it. Right-clicking selected text keeps the copy menu, and right-clicking a link keeps the link menu. On a phone, touch and hold a message to get the same actions in a sheet; tap outside it to close. Edited messages show (edited). You can edit or delete your own messages. Admins can also delete anyone's message in a channel or thread, or in a DM they are part of. They can edit messages the instance's bots posted, like a poll or an update note, and the edit shows as the bot's own. In channels and threads, admins are channel operators, so an IRC client gives them the same rights. Drafts save locally as you type. Switch conversations to find unsent text under Drafts in navigation; select one to continue at its end, or delete it there. Sending clears its entry.

title: Messages & media
heading: Deleting is not erasing
text: Deleting removes the message from server history, but IRC clients that already received it may keep their own copy.

title: Messages & media
heading: Images and videos
text: Use the attach button, drop, or paste to add up to 10 JPEG, PNG, or WebP photos, each under 12 MB. Attach or drop MP4, MOV, and WebM videos the same way. Before upload, your browser shrinks a large MP4 or MOV to about 720p and removes its location and other metadata. The video that uploads must be under 30 MB. Videos play inline with the player's own controls. Remove any of them with its × before sending. The server resizes each one to at most 1600 pixels on the longest edge and saves it as WebP, preserving transparency and removing embedded metadata. Your caption and photos go out as one message; if they do not fit in one message, each photo goes out as its own message, in order, with the caption on the first. Animated GIFs are not uploaded: send a GIF with /giphy. The GIF shows inline, with its bracketed [Giphy: …] label as the link; the original URL stays in the message for IRC clients. Every photo, video, and /giphy GIF keeps its box before its bytes arrive. Slirc knows each upload's pixel size, and a GIF carries its own in its link, so a channel full of pictures opens at the right height and nothing moves as they load. Collapse a message's image and embed previews to icons with the toggle on any preview. Slirc remembers collapsed messages per account in this browser. Private uploads require current conversation membership, including the parent conversation for thread media. Public-room media and custom emoji are public. See media access and its limits. Authorized video viewers can seek through the file. Open an image to zoom. Escape restores the normal view before closing it; reactions stay on the message, not in the lightbox.

title: Messages & media
heading: Links and previews
text: Paste a link and Slirc shows a preview with the page's title, description, and image when available. A link that points straight at an image, such as a Pexels photo, shows the picture inline instead of a card; click it to open the lightbox. When the server knows the picture's dimensions, Slirc reserves its space before it loads. A card's thumbnail always keeps the same frame, cropped to fill it, so a preview saved without a known size cannot shift the conversation either. Pages that publish oEmbed (YouTube, Vimeo, Spotify, SoundCloud, Bluesky, TikTok, Loom, CodePen, Figma, Apple Music, Bandcamp, Twitch, Mastodon and PeerTube instances) show a thumbnail with a play button; pressing it opens the player in a sandboxed frame. Privacy: preview images load through the Slirc server, and nothing is fetched from the provider by your browser until you press play. YouTube uses the no-cookie host, Vimeo gets do-not-track. Sites that need their own scripts (X, Instagram, Facebook) stay plain link cards. Previews are per device. Dismiss one with the × and Slirc remembers. A link to a message in this Slirc shows as a short label, such as View in #general, View in DM with sam or View in thread, and opens that message in place. Copy link in a message's menu copies a link anyone in that conversation can open in a browser, the desktop app or the phone app. It opens the conversation at that message, with the messages around it, even an old one, and the message glows briefly. On a message that started a reply thread, the link opens the thread too and shows as View thread in #general. A link to a reply opens its thread. A link to a DM message opens the same DM for both people in it, shown as View in DM with the other person. People who can't read the conversation, or a message that was deleted, get the note That message isn't available. In public rooms, you see the preview a member already loaded for that link, plus video thumbnails. The server does not fetch remote pages on request. Photos and videos pasted in those rooms stay visible to members too; private media requires current conversation membership.

title: Messages & media
heading: Links library
text: Some workspaces keep every shared link in a searchable library. It is off unless the workspace runs the links helper. When it's on, links saves each link posted in a channel it's in, once per link, with its title, preview image and a copy of the page text. The library lives in #links, which opens on a search field with the saved links grouped by day. Other channels with the helper in them get a Links and Messages switch in the header, showing that channel's links. A link from an invite-only channel is visible only to that channel's members. /link https://example.com/article saves a link to #links. /links opens the library, and /links followed by words searches it. Both commands show only where the helper runs.

title: Messages & media
heading: Searching a conversation
text: Press Cmd/Ctrl + F, or use the magnifying glass in the header, to search the open channel, DM or Notes. Type words to find messages that contain all of them, or add from:@name to limit results to one person. Pick a result to jump to that message; replies open their thread. Search covers the messages this device has loaded. Choose Load older messages to fetch more history.

title: Messages & media
heading: Commands
text: /help inside the app lists everything. The useful ones: Command What it does /help Browse the command list /me action Send an action ("waves") /msg nick text Open a direct message /threads [reply] Start a thread from the latest message /giphy search Find a GIF and send it /whois nick Look up a person /invite @nick or /invite email Add someone to this channel, or invite them by email /kick @nick [reason] Remove someone from a channel (admins only, see channels) /remind when text Set a reminder; it arrives in your DM with remind /poll question? a, b Start a poll; /poll 2 votes privately /reconnect Reconnect to IRC /leave Sign out of Slirc on this device

title: Messages & media
heading: Next
text: Turn one message into a focused conversation with threads, or tune when you get pinged in notifications.

title: Threads
text: Reply to any message in a side panel without cluttering the channel. Replies use standard IRCv3 `+reply` tags, so IRC clients see them in the same channel or DM.

title: Threads
heading: Start a thread in the app
text: Use a message's Reply in thread action (or press T on a selected message, or right-click a message on desktop). A thread panel opens beside the channel on desktop, or full-screen on a phone, showing the opening message and its replies. Replies stay inside the thread panel by default. Check Also send to #channel (or the DM name) before sending to post a copy to the main timeline as well. Press Esc or close the panel to return to the conversation. Messages with replies show a reply count under the message; select it to open the thread. On IRC, every reply travels in the same channel or DM with an IRCv3 +reply=<msgid> tag pointing to the opening message, so any IRC client can read and reply without joining a separate channel. The Threads group in the sidebar lists the threads you started or replied to, newest activity first, each with its opening text and channel. A count shows replies you haven't read. It lists the first three and a "more" row for the rest. Select a row to open the thread. Threads in a channel you leave drop off your list, and the group is hidden while you have none. A thread appears once one of its replies has reached the app.

title: Threads
heading: Use threads from IRC
text: For reply threads, standard IRC clients see each reply in the same channel or DM with an IRCv3 +reply=<msgid> tag. Clients that support +reply link replies back to the opening message automatically.

title: Notifications
text: Slirc can notify you about messages in your channels and DMs, even when the app is closed.

title: Notifications
heading: Turning them on
text: Open More → Profile on a phone. On desktop, open your profile from the rooms panel. Choose Change beside Notifications to turn them on, then allow notifications when your browser asks. Opening your profile does not request permission. If notifications are blocked, allow them in this site's browser settings, then reopen your profile. On iPhone, add Slirc to your Home Screen and open it there. Web push needs HTTPS and a browser that supports it. The Mac app and the iPhone app don't show notifications yet. For notifications on a computer, install Slirc from the browser; Download shows how.

title: Notifications
heading: Turning them off
text: Choose Change beside Notifications on your profile to turn them off. Off applies to every browser subscribed to your account. Turning notifications on enables this device and restores all-message notifications for your account. If you previously selected mentions-only in the legacy client, that preference stays in place until you use this switch. Notifications only arrive for channels you're a member of, and you won't be notified about your own messages. Multiline messages are bundled into one notification.

title: Notifications
heading: The daily G'day
text: Each morning @welcome posts a G'day gif in #open-chat. To stop seeing it, choose Change beside G'day greeting in #open-chat on your profile. Off hides the greeting in #open-chat, leaves it out of your unread count, and stops its notification. The first greeting you see has a note under it with Turn off and Keep, shown once per account. The setting follows your account to every device. Everyone else still sees the greeting, and @welcome's other messages stay visible. Reminders from @remind arrive in your DM with remind, never in a channel. While Slirc is open on another conversation, a reminder also shows a toast that stays until you choose Open or Dismiss. For a Remind me reminder the button is the message link, such as View in #general.

title: Notifications
heading: Unread counts
text: Channels, DMs and threads show how many new messages you haven't read. Reading one on a device clears its count on your other devices when the server keeps your read position. Otherwise each device keeps its own count.

title: Notifications
heading: Muting a conversation
text: Mute in a channel or DM menu dims its mark in navigation on this device and hides its unread count, including its threads. It does not change push notifications. Use your profile to turn push notifications off. Mute and unmute are per device. Muting on your phone does not mute your laptop. The public channels, #open-chat and #help, start muted.

title: Notifications
heading: Read next
text: See privacy & safety for where your data lives and who can see it.

title: Privacy & safety
text: Slirc runs on your operator's own hardware and talks an open protocol. This page names what is stored, what is gated, and where the edges are. This page describes how a Slirc instance handles your data. Every instance runs the same code under its own operator.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: Your data lives on the instance you chose
text: Conversations, identity, channels, and history stay on the machine your operator runs, the same one that serves the app. Slirc runs without third-party chat platforms, analytics, or tracking scripts. Because Slirc speaks IRC, your history is portable. Any IRC client can read it.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: Email and invitations
text: Your email address is not shown in chat, profiles or member lists. Slirc uses it for sign-in and invitations. When you invite someone by email, the invitation shows your name and email address so they can tell it is really you. A verified member who enters your exact email to start a conversation can discover your account through the resulting DM or membership. Slirc does not provide an email directory or email autocomplete. Senders can see addresses they entered in their own Invitations page. People search is not an instance directory. It returns only someone you can already discover: an explicit member of a public or workspace channel, someone who has posted in one (including #open-chat and #help), a person you share a non-direct room with that you both read, or someone you have a DM with, even a closed one. Posting in an open channel makes someone searchable but does not make them a Contact. A stranger who belongs only to a room you cannot see never appears, and guessing their account ID gets the same unavailable result as an unknown one. The address is also the key to your account, so you can't edit it yourself. Ask an admin to update it from your profile. Your next sign-in link goes to the new address.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: Channels are gated, twice
text: Invite-only channels stay hidden until you're invited, and the instance blocks anyone who isn't on the member list. Open channels are visible to every registered user, so anything you post there is group-wide. On a public instance, recent #open-chat messages are also readable without signing in at /open-chat: messages with their nick, time, reactions, polls and media posted there, and the avatars of people who posted. Member lists, presence, other channels, and who voted for what stay private. An archived channel is read-only. The public help channel, #help, is readable by signed-in members. Slirc does not currently offer anonymous reading there, and the member list stays hidden in the app for everyone: joins, parts, and quits aren't visible, and neither is the list of who's there. Slirc does not yet promise IRC invisibility.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: Agents read what a member reads
text: An agent runs on its owner's computer, and what it reads may go to the model provider its owner chose. It reads its DM with its owner and the open or invite-only channels its owner added it to. In an open channel it is owner-only and acts only on messages from its owner's account. Like a person you add, it can read each channel's full history, not only what comes after it joins. It leaves a channel when its owner does. Admins can see and remove every agent on the instance.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: Media follows conversation access
text: Uploads have random URLs. Photos and videos in private conversations require current membership, even when someone has the link. Thread media also requires access to its parent conversation. Losing membership blocks new requests, including video ranges; it cannot erase a copy someone already downloaded. Media posted in public rooms is public. Giphy and other externally hosted media follow their provider's access rules, not Slirc membership. Saving an image as custom emoji makes the cropped emoji public across this Slirc instance, including public rooms. Use an image everyone may see.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: Closing a DM is not deleting it
text: Close DM hides a one-to-one conversation from your list across devices. The other participant keeps seeing it, and its shared channel, membership, and history stay unchanged. A new message in it reopens it, and opening the person from Contacts also restores the DM and its history. Deleting a message is separate. It removes that message from server history. IRC clients that already received it may keep their own copy. That's the nature of an open protocol, and no product setting can undo it.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: Be careful with keys
text: Email invitations are personal. They expire after seven days, can be cancelled, and only the verified account for the invited email address can accept one. Media links point to files. Private uploads still require conversation membership; public-room files and custom emoji do not. Only share them with people you trust to be in the channel.

title: Privacy & safety
heading: FAQ
text: Who can read the public channels? Members signed in to Slirc can read `#help`. Slirc does not currently offer anonymous reading there, and joining events stay hidden in the app. On a public instance, anyone can read recent `#open-chat` messages at `/open-chat` without signing in. Can other people see my email? Your email is not listed in chat, profiles or member lists. Someone who enters your exact email can discover your account when Slirc opens a conversation or adds you to a channel. Senders can see addresses they entered in their own invitation history. An email invitation shows the sender's name and email address to the person invited. Who can open an uploaded image or video? Current members of the private conversation, including the parent of a thread. Public-room media and custom emoji are public. Removing access cannot erase copies already downloaded. Does Slirc track me? Slirc includes no analytics or tracking. Conversations stay on your operator's hardware.

title: IRC clients
text: Slirc remains IRC underneath, so the conversation does not depend on one client. Everything Slirc shows in the app is also on the IRC server. This page is for people who want a terminal or desktop client next to the PWA, or instead of it.

title: IRC clients
heading: Client shortlist
text: Client Platforms Interface Source Good fit for Senpai Linux, macOS terminal open a focused keyboard-driven client Halloy Linux, macOS, Windows desktop open a modern cross-platform GUI Textual macOS, iOS native commercial a polished Apple client Revolution IRC Android native open lightweight mobile IRC WeeChat Linux, macOS, BSD terminal open scripting and deep customization These clients support registered IRC accounts through SASL. Exact history and media presentation varies by client.

title: IRC clients
heading: How Slirc features appear
text: Channels remain ordinary IRC conversations. PWA direct messages appear as private #dm-* channels in terminal clients, so offline messages persist without fake presence. Email invitations only deliver the link. Whoever accepts is a normal account with normal channel access, so /list, auto-join and history behave as in any other room. Thread replies arrive in the same channel or DM with an IRCv3 +reply tag. Images, videos, GIFs, and previews remain readable URLs. Topics use the standard IRC topic. Edits and reactions use IRCv3 metadata. Halloy renders reactions under their message; clients without reaction support ignore them.

title: IRC clients
heading: How to connect
text: Nick Server name Server name is the local label in your IRC client. The connection still goes to chat.example.com. The commands and config below update as you type. Values stay in this browser. The in-app IRC clients tab fills in a workspace-specific server name (such as slirc-yourteam) for Halloy and WeeChat so multiple workspaces do not collide.

title: IRC clients
heading: Connect with a password
text: Open More → Profile → IRC clients on a phone, or Profile → IRC on desktop. Choose Use a password and name the device, for example Halloy on MacBook. Save the password when it appears. Slirc shows it once. Copy the setup block for your client. Clients connect to chat.example.com on port 6697 with TLS and SASL PLAIN. Adding or removing a password device rotates the account password, and so does New password, which makes one without adding a device. Older password clients must use the newest password before they can reconnect. For Halloy, add this to config.toml: [servers.{{server}}] server = "chat.example.com" port = 6697 use_tls = true nickname = "{{nick}}" username = "{{nick}}" [servers.{{server}}.sasl.plain] username = "{{nick}}" password = "the password Slirc showed you"

title: IRC clients
heading: Local development endpoint
text: A local development instance advertises its own IRC endpoint instead of chat.example.com, such as 127.0.0.1:6797, and the generated blocks use that host and port. A loopback address only works on the machine running the stack; another computer cannot reach it. That local Ergo uses a self-signed certificate, so the generated Halloy block adds dangerously_accept_invalid_certs = true with a warning comment. It accepts only this local certificate and must not be copied into a production config. Other clients get the same host and port but no certificate bypass; they need their own way to trust the local certificate, or the TLS handshake fails.

title: IRC clients
heading: Quiet server events in Halloy
text: Halloy shows IRC joins, leaves, mode changes, and kicks in channel history. To keep Slirc conversations focused, add this optional block. It only hides these events for the server name above; ordinary messages remain visible. [buffer.server_messages.change_mode] exclude = { servers = ["{{server}}"] } [buffer.server_messages.join] exclude = { servers = ["{{server}}"] } [buffer.server_messages.part] exclude = { servers = ["{{server}}"] } [buffer.server_messages.quit] exclude = { servers = ["{{server}}"] } [buffer.server_messages.kick] exclude = { servers = ["{{server}}"] }

title: IRC clients
heading: Connect with a certificate
text: A certificate gives each client its own credential. Revoking one certificate does not interrupt other clients. Generate an ECDSA P-256 key and self-signed certificate: nick={{nick}}; server={{server}}; openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 -nodes -days 3650 -subj "/CN=$nick" -keyout "$server-$nick.key" -out "$server-$nick.crt" && cat "$server-$nick.key" "$server-$nick.crt" > "$server-$nick.pem" && chmod 600 "$server-$nick.key" "$server-$nick.pem" && openssl x509 -in "$server-$nick.crt" -noout -fingerprint -sha256 Keep .key and .pem private. Anyone with either file can sign in as you. Open Profile → IRC → Use a certificate, name the device, and paste the SHA-256 fingerprint printed by OpenSSL.

title: IRC clients
heading: Halloy
text: Add this to Halloy's config.toml, using absolute paths: [servers.{{server}}] server = "chat.example.com" port = 6697 use_tls = true nickname = "{{nick}}" username = "{{nick}}" [servers.{{server}}.sasl.external] cert = "/path/to/{{server}}-{{nick}}.crt" key = "/path/to/{{server}}-{{nick}}.key"

title: IRC clients
heading: WeeChat
text: Copy the combined PEM to WeeChat's private certificate directory, then configure server: /server add {{server}} chat.example.com/6697 -tls /set irc.server.{{server}}.nicks "{{nick}}" /set irc.server.{{server}}.tls_cert "%h/tls/{{server}}-{{nick}}.pem" /set irc.server.{{server}}.sasl_mechanism external /connect {{server}} Older WeeChat releases call tls_cert ssl_cert and use -ssl instead of -tls.

title: IRC clients
heading: Textual
text: Convert certificate to PKCS #12, import it into macOS Keychain, then select identity certificate in Textual's server settings and choose SASL EXTERNAL: openssl pkcs12 -export -inkey {{server}}-{{nick}}.key -in {{server}}-{{nick}}.crt -out {{server}}-{{nick}}.p12 Textual on iOS must receive identity through iOS certificate/profile management before it appears in server settings. Textual versions without SASL EXTERNAL must use password setup above.

title: IRC clients
heading: Senpai
text: Senpai currently supports SASL PLAIN only and has no client-certificate setting. Use Use a password in Slirc for Senpai. Do not add PEM paths to Senpai config; current releases ignore them. Never enter your magic-link URL into an IRC client. Magic links sign in to web app. IRC clients use password or certificate from device setup.

title: About Slirc
text: Keep the parts of Slack that help conversation, lose the weight, and put IRC underneath it. Slack's interaction model on top of IRC. That was the whole idea.

title: About Slirc
heading: It started on a Friday
text: I met three friends at Lokaalhost:22. We spent a few hours comparing agentic workflows and swapping tools, and left with more energy than we arrived with. I wanted that conversation to continue. Signal did not work because one person was not there. WhatsApp was full of unrelated groups, tied to Meta, and easy to ignore. Slack had reactions, GIFs, and threads, but also a large Electron client, a short free-history window, and another subscription waiting down the road. We all use terminals. Why not IRC? My earliest memories of talking to people online are BBSs and IRC. IRC has survived for decades because it is simple, open, and good at moving messages between people. Servers once ran on machines far weaker than a cheap VPS today. I also tried Campfire. It was closer in spirit, but still larger than what I wanted. I wanted the useful parts of Slack with IRC doing the actual work.

title: About Slirc
heading: Slack where useful, IRC everywhere else
text: The web app handles images, videos, link previews, reactions, notifications, direct messages, and threads. Underneath, the conversation remains IRC. Open Slirc in Halloy, Senpai, mIRC, or another IRC client and the channel still makes sense. An image becomes a URL. A thread becomes another channel. Nothing depends on one interface understanding a private format. The main client is a PWA. Save it to a phone and it behaves like an installed app without an app store or a large native download. I built it for the phone first. The stack. Slirc uses Bun, Hono, Alpine.js, SQLite, and Ergo. Ergo owns IRC accounts, channels, permissions, chat history, and reactions. The app keeps the metadata needed for profiles, invites, uploads, notifications, reminders, and polls. I chose tools I can understand and operate myself. Fewer moving pieces means lower memory use and less work when something breaks. Slirc is free to run yourself, on your own server, under the Elastic License 2.0. The FAQ has the details. Campfire vs Slirc has the current resource numbers.

title: About Slirc
heading: Channels and access
text: Only members post in #open-chat and #help. On the public instance, a visitor who isn't signed in can read recent #open-chat messages at /open-chat, and nothing else. Open channels are listed for every member to join. Invite-only channels stay hidden until someone invites you. Email is the front door: new members join from an invite link and pick a name, and returning members sign in with a magic link. On the public instance, a new email address can also sign up from the sign-in form; the account starts once the emailed link or code proves the address, and it belongs only to #open-chat and #help until someone invites it. IRC still enforces the channel boundaries. Threads that remain IRC. Threads were the interesting constraint. How do you isolate one discussion without inventing something ordinary IRC clients cannot read? A Slirc thread is a channel linked to its opening message. The app presents it as a focused conversation. An IRC client presents it as another room. Both are true. That pattern guides the rest of the product: improve the interface and keep the protocol. Formatting and media. Messages support the formatting I use: bold, emphasis, inline code, and fenced code blocks with syntax highlighting. Photos upload from the composer and GIFs come from /giphy. Links get previews, and YouTube, Vimeo, and other oEmbed links get a player. Outside the PWA, all of that reads as plain text and URLs.

title: About Slirc
heading: Editing without pretending
text: Messages can be edited and deleted in the app. Deleting removes a message from server history, but an IRC client that already received it may keep a copy. Slirc says so up front. Modern controls are useful, but IRC remains the source of truth.

title: About Slirc
heading: Why the .org
text: I bought slirc.org because I want this to become something other people can run. Host it yourself, keep your data, and contribute fixes back. A hosted version may make sense too, because convenience is worth paying for even when the underlying software is available. The first useful version took a couple of days and a few dollars in model credits. Producing code was the easy part. The hard part is deciding what belongs, what stays understandable in IRC, and what should be removed. That is still the work.

title: Agents
text: Connect a coding session you already have open. It gets its own name and a direct message with you, and acts only on your messages.

title: Agents
heading: Which agents work today
text: Pi, Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode work with Slirc today. Harness Status Pi Works today Claude Code Works today Codex Works today OpenCode Works today

title: Agents
heading: Requirements
text: Install Pi, Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode on the computer. You also need Node 18 or newer, or Bun. The Claude Code and Codex setups run on macOS and Linux. For Claude Code, the claude command must be on your path, and the version must be 2.1.286 or newer. Slirc needs that version to load its plugin. If slirc-agent says yours is older, run claude update, then run the command again. For Codex, the codex command must be on your path, version 0.169 to 0.172. Slirc delivers your messages through the Codex background service that a plain codex start uses. Codex skips that service when it starts with --no-daemon, -c, --profile, --enable, --disable or --oss, and a session started that way can't connect. If slirc-agent says your Codex version isn't one it knows, it also says what to run. For OpenCode, you need version 2.3 (opencode --version shows it). OpenCode 1.x doesn't work with Slirc. Install OpenCode 2 with npm install -g @opencode/cli, then run the command again.

title: Agents
heading: Connect a session
text: Open Agents (Profile → Agents on desktop, More → Agents on a phone) and copy the command. It names your workspace and ends with a connect code, for example: bunx slirc-agent@latest calango Xk3fP9qLm2aB The page adds the connect code when you press the copy button, so copy with the button rather than selecting the text. The code only tells Slirc whose Agents page to show the request on, and it lasts two minutes. If it expired, the session says so. Copy the command again, or open the link the session shows. npx slirc-agent@latest calango Xk3fP9qLm2aB works the same if you use npm; Use npx on the Agents page switches the command. On app.slirc.org the workspace is app.slirc.org. Paste the command into a running Pi, Claude Code or OpenCode session as your own message, and let the agent run it. It sets up Slirc for that agent and connects that same session: If Slirc was already set up, the link and code show in the session as soon as the command ends. The first time, or after an update, it asks you to type /reload in Pi or /reload-plugins in Claude Code. The link and code show right after. OpenCode needs nothing typed: the command reloads it. You don't type /slirc (or slirc in Codex). Slirc connects the session only when your own latest message was that command for the same workspace. If the agent runs the command on its own, say because a file told it to, nothing connects, and the session shows a notice telling you what to type if you meant it. Run the command in a terminal instead and it sets up the agent and starts it in that folder, ready to connect. If more than one of them is installed, it asks which one to start. Codex needs the terminal. Run the command in the folder you want Codex to work in. Pasted into Codex, the command runs in Codex's sandbox without asking you, and the sandbox can't download it. From a terminal it sets up Slirc for Codex and starts Codex with slirc calango and the connect code already typed, so the link and code show in Codex and your Agents page shows the request by itself. The first time, Codex asks you to review Slirc's hooks before it starts. Choose Trust all and continue. The Agents page shows Waiting for your agent… after you copy, then the request by itself: the agent, session name, folder and machine, plus a code. The session shows the same 8-character code, in two groups of four, next to a link. Choose Allow if the codes match, or Deny if they don't. Nothing is connected until you allow it. If the page doesn't show the request, type or paste the code into Code from your agent, under the command, or open the link from the session, on any device where you're signed in. Stray spaces in a pasted code are fine. After that, connect another session on the same computer by pasting the command again, or by typing /slirc calango in it (/slirc once the computer knows your workspace). In Codex, run the command in a terminal again, or type slirc calango with no slash, since Codex rejects commands it doesn't know. A session you connected before reconnects by itself when you reopen it. If you already have your own /slirc command or skill in Claude Code, it keeps that name. Slirc's command becomes /slirc-connect instead. Codex asks you to review Slirc's hooks the first time it starts with them, and again after every Slirc update. Choose Trust all and continue. Without that, Slirc's hooks don't run and the session can't connect. You can also trust them later under /hooks. Codex loads Slirc in every folder, and a session starts nothing until you connect it. To resume a Codex session later, run codex resume <id>. It reconnects without pairing again. Claude Code loads Slirc only in the folder where you ran slirc-agent. Claude Code writes that setting to .claude/settings.local.json in the folder. Sessions in other folders start without Slirc. The first time you use a new folder, Claude Code asks whether to trust it. Accept, or Slirc can't load there. To resume a Claude Code session later, run claude --resume <id> in the same folder. It reconnects without pairing again. OpenCode keeps its sessions in a background service that stays up after you quit it. Slirc counts an OpenCode session as online only while an OpenCode window shows it, as the open session or a tab. Quit OpenCode or close the tab and the agent shows offline. Open the session again, with opencode -c for the last one or opencode -s <id>, and it reconnects. A workspace is the part before .slirc.app. For a self-hosted Slirc, use the full address, such as npx slirc-agent@latest chat.example.com. Run npx slirc-agent@latest --help to see every option, and npx slirc-agent@latest status to see what's set up on this computer. If more than one tool is installed, slirc-agent asks which one to use. --harness pi, --harness claude, --harness codex or --harness opencode picks one directly. If the workspace runs a newer Slirc than your copy of slirc-agent, the command says so and prints the exact version to run. The agent shows up under Agents in your sidebar once you allow it. Each session you connect is its own agent with its own direct message. The DM header uses the same session name as the sidebar, with the harness and stable nick underneath, for example Pi · pi-4223, Claude Code · claude-8fe7 or Codex · codex-e186. An unnamed session uses its nick as the title. Want Slirc to work with another coding agent? See app/agent/HARNESSES.md in the repository for the harness interface and checklist.

title: Agents
heading: When a session goes offline
text: A session that closes or sleeps shows as offline. A Codex session goes offline when you close its window, even though Codex can keep it in the background, and comes back when you reopen it with codex resume <id>. About two minutes after it goes offline, the agent leaves a card in its direct message. For Claude Code, the card reads "Claude Code session offline" and shows the resume command, cd '<folder>' && claude --resume <id>, with a copy button. Its Remove button opens the Agents page, where you can delete the agent. Messages sent while the session is offline wait for you to confirm them after it reconnects.

title: Agents
heading: Talking to it
text: Write in its direct message, or /invite it to an open or invite-only channel and mention it there. An open-channel attachment is owner-only: it acts only on messages from your account, checked by the IRC account tag, and someone else mentioning it there is context, never work. Replies go back where you asked. What you do in the terminal stays in the terminal. This agent can read the channel's full history, the same as a person you add, and it may pass what it reads to your model provider. Threads started there later include it. When you leave the channel, or an admin removes you, your agent leaves it and its threads too. In a Pi agent's DM, Queued beside your message means it is waiting to run, including behind work already happening in the terminal. Working appears only when Pi starts that request. The label clears after Slirc confirms the reply, or when the connection or request can no longer be verified. These labels describe agent work, not message delivery. If you stop a turn while it works on a Slirc request (Esc in OpenCode), the request ends with "The agent was stopped before replying." If OpenCode shows a Slirc request with the spinner running and nothing changes, the model has stopped answering. Press Esc to stop that turn. Requests that arrived in the meantime stay in OpenCode's queue and run after your next message, so type anything, such as continue. If it happens again, pick another model with /models. The agent runs on your machine, so it keeps its files, context and permission prompts.

title: Agents
heading: Rename or remove
text: Rename changes the name in Slirc and, where the harness allows it, in the session too. Remove revokes the agent's account, channel access and direct message. It may not stop work already running locally. Admins see every member's agents on the Admin page and can remove any of them. Removing a member also removes their agents. For a script that only posts, use a bot instead.

title: Bots
text: A bot is an IRC account your own script logs in as. Slirc also runs its own helpers for reminders, help and polls.

title: Bots
heading: What a bot is
text: Slirc does not run your code. A bot is a normal IRC account with a name you choose. Your script connects to the IRC server with that name and password, joins channels, and sends messages. What it says appears in Slirc and in every other IRC client. Use a bot when the thing speaking isn't you in a conversation, such as a build server, a status page or a script that answers one question. For work you drive yourself, connect a personal agent.

title: Bots
heading: Create a bot
text: Admins create bots on the Admin page, under Bots. Type a name and choose Create bot. Slirc shows the bot's password once, with a Copy button. Put it in your script, then choose Done; the password can't be shown again. Lost a password, or think it leaked? Choose New password on the bot's row. The old one stops working at once and the new one appears once, the same way. Remove deletes the bot's IRC account and takes it out of every channel. Bot names are shared with people and agents, so a name that is already taken becomes name-yournick.

title: Bots
heading: Connect your script
text: Clients connect to chat.example.com on port 6697 with TLS and SASL PLAIN: nick: the bot's name password: the password Slirc showed you Any IRC client library works, in any language, because the bot is an ordinary IRC client.

title: Bots
heading: Invite it to a channel
text: A bot joins a channel the same way a person does: /invite @deploy-yournick A note appears at the bottom of the channel, Add @deploy-yournick to #yourchannel?, with Add and Dismiss. Choose Add and the bot joins. Only you see the note. Anyone in the channel can add it. After that the bot reads and posts there like any other member, and Slirc marks it with a bot badge.

title: Bots
heading: Reminders, help, and polls: @remind, @help, @poll
text: @remind, @help and @poll are helpers Slirc runs for you. A fourth, @welcome, lives in #open-chat and posts a daily G'day gif there, which you can hide for yourself on your profile (see notifications). Each server picks which helpers it runs, so one you don't see in / may be off on yours. Just mention the helper. For @help and @poll, if the helper isn't in the channel yet, a note under your message says @poll isn't in #design. (or names the group) with Add and Dismiss. Choose it and the helper joins and answers the message you already sent, so you don't send it again. Only you see the note, and a helper never joins without that click. /invite @poll adds it ahead of time. Helpers can't join DMs with other people or threads. A message that starts with @remind is private: Slirc sets the reminder for you, shows the confirmation as a notice, and does not post the message in the channel. @remind never needs to join a channel. @remind keeps a schedule of reminders. Exact times work without a model, and configured instances also understand natural phrasing: @remind in 20m stretch @remind tomorrow 9:00 pick up cake @remind next Friday morning call Mum @remind list @remind cancel 1 /remind in 20m stretch does the same thing. @remind list or /remind list opens your DM with @remind and posts your next six reminders there, one per line, and says when more remain. Each line shows when it fires, such as Tomorrow at 9:00 or In 20 minutes, 14:32 on your clock, then what it's about, then a link back to the message when it came from Remind me. The numbers reflect the current list, starting at 1; cancel one with @remind cancel 1. To remember a message, open its ⋮ menu (on a phone, press and hold the message) and choose Remind me, then pick In 20 minutes, In 1 hour or Tomorrow at 9:00. Slirc sets the reminder with a short quote and a link back to the message, and the confirmation shows as a notice. When it fires, the quote shows as a quote block with a short link such as View in #general that opens the message. Custom… shows a date and time field instead, set to the next full hour; pick any time within the next year and choose Set reminder, or Back to return to the times. Reminders always arrive in your DM with @remind, never in a channel, even when you asked in one. Slirc opens that DM for you if it isn't there yet. The confirmation is a notice only you see, with the time on your clock, such as Reminder at 14:32 (in 20 minutes): stretch or Reminder tomorrow at 9:00: pick up cake. From an IRC client such as Halloy, an @remind line in a channel is posted like any message, but the answer comes as a private notice and the reminder links back to that line. If Slirc is open on another conversation when a reminder arrives, a toast like Reminder: stretch stays until you choose Open to go to the DM or Dismiss. A Remind me toast quotes the message, and its button is the short link instead, such as View in #general. Slirc confirms delivery from the server's own echo of the message, not from the send. If a restart leaves the outcome unknown, Slirc sends the reminder once more on its own only when it can prove the first one never arrived. Otherwise @remind list marks it may not have sent, and @remind resend 1 sends it again; it may then arrive twice. Reminders created before this confirmation existed show the same way. Cancelling one stops any further attempt, but a message that already went out cannot be retracted. @help answers questions about Slirc from these guides, and links the section it used: @help how do email invitations work? @help can guests read #help? In #help it answers without a mention. If a question is not covered by the guides, it says so rather than guessing, and a question about something other than Slirc gets a short line saying it only knows Slirc.
